1|5-Step Sign-Up Process.trainee_content:
The 5 Steps are the backbone of every conversation: Introduction, Present the Problem, The Solution, The Close, Rehash. You run them in the right order, every time, without skipping a step. It should sound confident and natural, never like a script.

The order matters because each step earns the next one. When a close falls flat, it's almost always because a step got skipped.
what_good_looks_like: Runs the full sign-up process in order, no steps missed
Sounds confident and natural, not rehearsed
Each step earns the next — no jumping straight to the close
how_measured: Office roleplay: all five steps, in order, without being prompted
Watch a live pitch in the field
Ask them which step a stalled conversation got stuck on
leader_coaching_notes: Drill the order until it's automatic, then coach how it sounds
If it sounds scripted, roleplay with interruptions until it bends without breaking
After live pitches, walk back through step by step — where was the miss?

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain the 5-Step Sign-Up Process in simple words, and why the order matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me the 5-Step Sign-Up Process — in roleplay, then on a live pitch.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you run the 5 steps every day, not just when I'm watching?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you use the 5 steps without anyone reminding you?

1|Accurate Body Positioning.trainee_content:
Your body pitches before your mouth does. Stand in the right spot. Keep your posture open, confident, and engaging. Use your hands and gestures to build trust and show energy.

Always respect personal space. Where you stand decides whether the conversation even starts.
what_good_looks_like: Stands in the right spot so the conversation opens naturally
Open, confident posture — hands and gestures build trust
Respects personal space at all times
how_measured: Watch their positioning in the field across the day
Roleplay: approach angle, stance, and distance
Stop-rate shows whether the positioning is working
leader_coaching_notes: Walk the patch and physically place them — you coach this by doing it
Mirror their stance back to them; nobody can see their own posture
Watch the distance: trust dies when you're too far AND too close

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain body positioning in simple words, and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me your positioning — in roleplay, then on a live approach.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Is your positioning right every day, not just some days?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you get your positioning right without being reminded?

1|Clear Close.trainee_content:
Interest is not a result — commitment is. You close clearly and with confidence, turning the supporter's interest into a real commitment.

No trailing off. No hoping they offer it themselves. Be direct, slow down, hold eye contact, ask for the long term — then tell them what happens next. You ask cleanly, then you stay comfortable in the silence that follows.
what_good_looks_like: Closes clearly and confidently — turns interest into real commitment
Asks for the sign-up directly instead of waiting for it to be offered
Stays comfortable with the silence after the ask
how_measured: Roleplay: the close gets asked out loud, not hinted at
Field watch: how many interested conversations turn into sign-ups
Sign-ups where the supporter knew exactly what they agreed to
leader_coaching_notes: Most new starters talk right past the close — coach the stop
Drill three clean closing lines until one feels natural
Debrief the 'almosts': was the close actually asked?

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain what a clear close is, and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me a clear close — in roleplay, then on a live pitch.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you close clearly every day, not just now and then?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you go for the close without anyone pushing you to?

1|Communicates Clearly.trainee_content:
Clear communication is a skill, and you get better at it on purpose. Keep your updates clear. When something goes wrong, raise it the right way — right person, right time, right tone.

A team runs on information. Yours should be the kind people can trust and act on.
what_good_looks_like: Keeps updates clear — short, accurate, on time
Raises issues the right way, professionally
Right person, right time, right tone
how_measured: Quality of daily check-ins and end-of-day updates
Look at how they raised their last issue
No surprises: problems come from them first
leader_coaching_notes: Give the update format once — what happened, the numbers, what's blocking
Praise a well-raised issue out loud; the whole team learns from it
Coach tone and content separately — both matter

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain what clear communication looks like here, and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me: give me a proper update, or raise an issue the right way.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are your updates clear every day, not just when things are easy?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you communicate well without being chased for it?

1|Emotional Regulation in the Field.trainee_content:
Being steady is a choice you make before the day tests you. You stay solid when the day gets hard, and you keep your personal life separate from your work performance.

The field never finds out what kind of morning you had.
what_good_looks_like: Stays steady even when the day gets hard
Keeps personal stuff separate from work performance
Steady presence — teammates can't read a bad day off them
how_measured: Watch them on high days and low days
Composure in front of supporters when things go wrong
Effort stays the same no matter the results
leader_coaching_notes: Coach the pattern, never one bad moment
Model it yourself — steadiness is caught as much as taught
Give them a private way to reset on genuinely hard days

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain why staying steady in the field matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me you can stay steady — in roleplay pressure, and out on the doors.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you steady every day, good days and bad?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you keep yourself steady without anyone stepping in?

1|Field IQ.trainee_content:
Field IQ is the office's single source of truth — and it's only true if you feed it. Make Field IQ part of your daily routine: complete, accurate, no missing fields, every day.

Your numbers drive your coaching, your territory, and your earnings. A gap in the data is a gap in all three.
what_good_looks_like: Field IQ is part of the daily routine
Complete and accurate — no missing fields
Submitted every day without being chased
how_measured: Field IQ done with no missing fields (Stage 1 evidence item)
No data chase-ups across a full week
Spot-check: does the data match the day?
leader_coaching_notes: Do the first submissions together until the habit sticks
Show them THEIR data being used in a real coaching decision
Honest data is non-negotiable — hold that line absolutely

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain what Field IQ is for, and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me a complete, accurate Field IQ submission from your day.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Is your Field IQ in every day without anyone chasing you?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you submit Field IQ on your own, no reminders?

1|Follows Standards.trainee_content:
Standards are what you do when nobody's watching. You bring discipline and effort without needing someone over your shoulder or a pat on the back — and you know WGLL for quality standards and KPIs.

Following standards as a BA is your first rep at holding them at Stage 3.
what_good_looks_like: Brings discipline and effort with no one watching and no reward needed
Knows WGLL for quality standards and KPIs
Same standard whether the coach is there or not
how_measured: Compare an unannounced watch with an accompanied one — same person?
Quality KPIs hold up without prompting
Ask them: can they say the standards from memory?
leader_coaching_notes: Spell out the standards early — vague standards can't be followed
Catch them meeting the standard when they think nobody saw, and say so
Link today's discipline to tomorrow's leadership

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you tell me the standards from memory, and why they matter?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me you work to the standard — in roleplay and out in the field.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you hold the standard every day, watched or not?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you follow the standards without anyone checking on you?

1|Impulses.trainee_content:
Impulses are the reasons people act now instead of "maybe later." Ours are G.I.F.T.S: Generosity, Indifference, Feel Good Factor, Tone of Voice / Body Language, Support.

You should be able to say what each impulse is and what it does. Then work them into your conversation naturally — you know where each one fits and how to use it.

Used naturally, impulses build momentum. Forced, they just feel like pressure. Keep them natural.
what_good_looks_like: Can name the impulses and say what each one does
Works them into the conversation naturally, not tacked on
Knows where and how each impulse should be used
how_measured: Verbal check: name the impulses and where each one belongs
Roleplay: impulses woven in without sounding forced
Watch live conversations — is there momentum?
leader_coaching_notes: Have them spot the impulses in YOUR pitch first
Coach one impulse at a time into their conversation
If anything drifts towards pressure, fix it right away

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you tell me what the impulses are and why they matter, in your own words?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me the impulses working in a roleplay — and can you do it live too?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are the impulses showing up in your pitches day after day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you use the impulses on your own, without anyone reminding you?

1|Law of Averages.trainee_content:
"The law of averages is not an excuse to be average. It is a reminder to control the inputs."

Put in steady inputs, and the outputs follow — you can count on it. Know your numbers. Trust your ratios. On a slow day, don't start doubting the process — keep feeding the top of the funnel. That's how you apply LOA to get steady results.
what_good_looks_like: Understands LOA and can explain it simply
Uses it to get steady results — inputs stay up on slow days
Trusts the ratios instead of riding the emotional rollercoaster
how_measured: Verbal check: explain LOA and their own current ratios
Activity stays steady through a low-conversion day
Uses LOA language when talking through results
leader_coaching_notes: Work out their personal ratios together from real data
On a slow day, point them back to inputs — LOA kills panic
Show the weekly view: the average always tells a calmer story

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain the Law of Averages to me simply, and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me how you use the Law of Averages in a roleplay and out in the field.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Does the Law of Averages guide your work day after day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you apply the Law of Averages on your own, without a prompt?

1|Professional Reliability.trainee_content:
Being reliable is the first professional skill. Respect start times and schedules. Show up prepared and ready to work.

Manage yourself so nobody has to remind you or chase you. When nothing about you needs chasing, people trust you — and that trust is what everything else gets built on.
what_good_looks_like: Respects start times and schedules — prepared and ready to work
Manages themselves without reminders or follow-up
The team can count on them every day, not most days
how_measured: On time and ready, day after day in a row
Zero chase-ups needed over a full week
Shows up the same on good days and bad days
leader_coaching_notes: Set the expectation once, clearly — then hold it every time
Praise reliability out loud; it's the habit everything builds on
One slip: coach same day. Pattern: retrain plan

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you tell me what professional reliability means here and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Are you showing up on time, prepared, and ready — in the office and in the field?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Have you been reliable day after day, in a row?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you manage yourself without anyone chasing or reminding you?

1|Quality KPIs.trainee_content:
Volume without quality is borrowed money — it comes back to bite you.

Know the quality KPIs and why hitting them matters: 70%+ Welcome Calls answered, 1st payment 85%+, 3rd payment 70%+. Then show the actions that keep sign-ups high quality: set the right expectations, capture the right details, and sign the right supporter for the right reasons.
what_good_looks_like: Can name the quality KPIs and say why they matter
Shows the actions that keep sign-ups high quality
Sets the right expectations so sign-ups stick
how_measured: Verbal check: name the quality KPIs and the habits behind them
Their own quality numbers over recent weeks
Watch a close: are expectations set correctly?
leader_coaching_notes: Tie quality to their own earnings — it's not abstract
Go through one of their sign-ups together against the quality checklist
Coach the habit behind a quality dip, not the number itself

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you name the quality KPIs and tell me why they matter?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me the actions that keep a sign-up high quality — in roleplay and live.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are your quality numbers holding up day after day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you protect quality on your own, without being told?

1|Question Handling.trainee_content:
A question is usually interest in disguise.

When a supporter raises a concern: listen first, use the systems, and find the real worry underneath — Feel, Relate, Felt, Found, Re-close. Then check the worry is gone before you re-close.

Answer the wrong question and you lose the sign-up — even when your answer was right.
what_good_looks_like: Listens first — finds the real worry under the question
Uses the systems instead of making up answers
Checks the worry is gone before re-closing
how_measured: Roleplay the concerns we can address: other charities, one-off, bank details, online, more information
Watch in the field: calm and structured when questioned
How often they re-close after handling a question
leader_coaching_notes: Teach the pattern: listen, answer, check, re-close
Drill Feel, Relate, Felt, Found, Re-close on each concern we can address
Coach listening — most BAs answer the wrong question

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain how to handle a question and why doing it right matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Handle a few tough questions for me in roleplay — can you do the same live?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you handling questions well day after day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you handle questions on your own, without a prompt?

1|Resilience After Rejection.trainee_content:
Rejection is the weather on the doors. It isn't about you.

Don't let one bad interaction touch the next one. Bounce back fast and reset for the next opportunity. Stay productive instead of getting emotional or down.

Results are one thing. Your attitude and effort are another — keep them separate.
what_good_looks_like: Doesn't let one bad interaction touch the next one
Bounces back fast and resets for the next opportunity
Stays productive instead of getting emotional or discouraged
Keeps results separate from attitude and effort
how_measured: Watch the pitch right AFTER a hard no
Activity holding up through a slow morning
How they talk about themselves after a rough session
leader_coaching_notes: Watch the recovery, not the rejection — that's where the coaching is
Teach the reset ritual: breathe, next door, fresh start
Make the numbers normal: rejection is the cost of every yes

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you tell me why bouncing back from rejection matters, in your own words?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me the reset — what does your next pitch look like after a hard no?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you bouncing back fast every day, not just some days?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you reset on your own after a no, without needing a push?

1|SEE Principle.trainee_content:
SEE stands for Smile, Eye contact, Enthusiasm. It's how you connect in the first seconds — before your words matter.

The person at the door can hear the smile in your voice. Your eye contact shows you're present and can be trusted. Your enthusiasm shows you truly believe in what you're talking about.

Win the first seconds and the rest of the conversation gets a chance.
what_good_looks_like: Connects right away, in the first seconds
The person at the door can hear the smile in your voice
Eye contact shows you are present and can be trusted
Enthusiasm shows real belief in what you're talking about
how_measured: Watch first impressions across several approaches in the field
Roleplay: can they switch SEE on right after a rejection?
Stop-rate holding steady through the day
leader_coaching_notes: Coach it physically — smile, posture, energy — not as theory
Watch the approach after a hard no: SEE is proven under rejection
Film a roleplay and let them see their own first three seconds

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you tell me what SEE stands for and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me SEE in a roleplay — and does it hold up live at the doors?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Is SEE switched on every day, all day — not just when you feel good?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you bring SEE on your own, without anyone prompting you?

1|Seeks Support Early & Proactively.trainee_content:
Struggling in silence costs you. When something's off, say it early — flag it, ask the question, use the support around you. Small problems get fixed fast.

Asking for help early is a strength, not a weakness. The best people in this business do it at every level.
what_good_looks_like: Flags problems early, while they're still small
Asks questions instead of guessing
Uses support the right way so problems get fixed fast
how_measured: How long between a problem showing up and them saying something
Do they ask questions in coaching? Silence is the warning sign
Are problems getting fixed while they're still cheap, or after they got expensive?
leader_coaching_notes: React well the first time they flag something — that decides if there's a second time
Ask 'what are you stuck on?' every day until they start telling you first
Tell them a real story of a problem that got expensive because someone hid it

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Why is asking for help early a strength, not a weakness?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me the last problem you flagged — how did you raise it?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you speak up early every day, or only when it's already bad?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you flag problems on your own, or wait until someone asks?

1|Stage 1 \u2014 The Foundation Standard.trainee_content:
Stage 1 is the base everything else sits on: the core skills of the role, learned for real and proven — not just sat through.

You work the material every day. You prove it in roleplay and in a live environment. Your coach signs off the proof.

You move up on evidence, never on time served.
what_good_looks_like: Evidence: three days in a row with great time ownership and effort
Evidence: runs the 5-step sign-up process and handles common objections in roleplay AND live
Evidence: Field IQ done with no missing fields
how_measured: Non-negotiables: attendance, professionalism, honesty, data submission
A missed standard means coaching right away and a same-day retrain plan
Miss the standard again and again, and progression pauses
leader_coaching_notes: Agree the evidence up front — the three items above are the sign-off
Tools used daily: Learning Library, Field IQ
Coach on a slipped standard the day it slips, never the week after

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What does Stage 1 stand for, and why do you move up on evidence, not time?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me the Stage 1 basics in roleplay and out live — can you prove them?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Have you hit the Stage 1 standard day after day, not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you hold the Stage 1 standard on your own, without being told?

2|Assuming the Role.trainee_content:
Start acting like a leader before you get the title. Own your standards, own your behaviour, and know that people are watching how you carry yourself.

Advancement doesn't make you a leader — it recognises one who already exists. Stage 2 is where you start being that person.
what_good_looks_like: Starts acting like a leader — owns their standards and behaviour
Knows the effect they have on others and uses it well
Steps up without being asked when the moment needs it
how_measured: Moments of leadership nobody asked for, seen by you
Newer BAs are visibly better for being around them
Owns outcomes when the team is together
leader_coaching_notes: Give them small leadership moments — a huddle, a new starter's first hour
Debrief their influence: who did you lift today?
Coach the difference between having the role and living it

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What does it mean to act like a leader before you have the title?
assessment_prompts.skill: When did you last step up without being asked? Walk me through it.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you showing leadership day after day, or only when it's easy?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you take ownership on your own, or wait for a push?

2|Clean Data You Can Trust.trainee_content:
Track your data right: no missing fields, no shortcuts. Your numbers should be ones people can trust without double-checking.

Bad data doesn't just fool you. It wastes your coach's time and the office's decisions. At Stage 2, your numbers are never the question.
what_good_looks_like: Tracks data right — no missing fields, no shortcuts
Enters data the same day, not from memory later
Numbers can be trusted without anyone double-checking
how_measured: Data audits come back clean
Nobody has to chase them for missing submissions
Spot-check: do their numbers match what really happened?
leader_coaching_notes: Spot-check monthly and tell them you do — trusted data is earned
Coach same-day entry: memory is where accuracy dies
Show them a real decision their data drove — make it matter

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Why does bad data cost more than just you?
assessment_prompts.skill: Open your numbers — would they pass a spot-check right now?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Is your data clean every day, or just when someone's looking?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you enter it same-day on your own, or do you get chased?

2|Close Variations.trainee_content:
One script is a ceiling. You know more than one way to close, and you use them with confidence — reading the person and adapting on the spot.

The redirect scripts — one-off, 'can I do it online?', 'it's only a small amount' — are close variations too. Different people say yes for different reasons. Your close should fit the person in front of you.
what_good_looks_like: Uses different closes with confidence, not one memorised script
Reads the person and adapts on the spot
Switches angle mid-conversation when the first close doesn't land
how_measured: Roleplay: same pitch, three different supporter types
Watch them in the field: which close did they pick and why
Close rate across different types of supporters
leader_coaching_notes: Name the closes together — shared words make coaching specific
Debrief real doors: which close, why, what else would have worked?
Drill the switch: first close misses, what now?

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Why do different supporters need different closes?
assessment_prompts.skill: Give me three closes for three different supporters, right now.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you switching closes every day out there, or falling back on one?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you pick the close yourself in the moment, without a prompt?

2|Daily Inputs & Weekly Outputs.trainee_content:
You can explain your performance in numbers, not feelings. You know the daily inputs it takes to hit your targets — doors, conversations, presentations — and you count them as the day runs, not at the end.

Outputs follow inputs. Every single week.
what_good_looks_like: Knows the daily inputs needed to hit their targets
Counts inputs as the day runs, not at the end
Explains performance in numbers, not feelings
how_measured: Can tell you today's input counts at any point in the day
The maths works: their inputs times their averages hits their targets
Weeks are planned in inputs, not hopes
leader_coaching_notes: Ask for their numbers at 2 PM, not 8 PM
Coach the maths: target divided by averages = today's inputs
Cut feelings-talk in debriefs — numbers first, then context

assessment_prompts.knowledge: How many doors and conversations do you need today to hit your target — and how do you know?
assessment_prompts.skill: What are your input counts right now, mid-day?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you track inputs live every day, or add them up at night?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you plan your week in inputs on your own, without being told?

2|GRASP.trainee_content:
You can say what G.R.A.S.P is for, and you show it in the office and in the field. It's about being the best example — preparing for real leadership:

Getting with the Right People · Responsibility · Attitude · Systems · Profit.

At Stage 2 it's not something you recite. It's something people can see in how you show up every day.
what_good_looks_like: Can say what GRASP is for
Shows it in the office and in the field
Others can see it in how they act, without being told
how_measured: Talk it through: can they explain the purpose, not just the letters?
Watch them in the office and in the field
What teammates say about them reflects it
leader_coaching_notes: Quiz the purpose, then point at real moments: where was GRASP just now?
Catch them living it and name it out loud in front of the team
Coach the gap between knowing it and living it

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What is GRASP for — in your own words?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me GRASP in a real moment today — where did it show up?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Would your teammates say you live GRASP every day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Does GRASP show in how you act without anyone reminding you?

2|Improved Question Handling.trainee_content:
At Stage 2, you handle questions clearly and in order no matter what's going on — rain, noise, a doubtful householder, a long day.

Listen for the real worry hiding under the question. Answer it using the system. Check the worry is gone. Then re-close.

No freezing. No making it up. One hard question should never knock your pitch off track.
what_good_looks_like: Answers questions clearly and in order, whatever the conditions
Finds the real worry under the question
Checks the worry is gone before re-closing
how_measured: Roleplay with curveball questions under pressure
Watch them in the field in different conditions
Conversion stays steady on hard-question days
leader_coaching_notes: Throw the ugliest questions in roleplay — the structure should survive
Coach listening first: most BAs answer the wrong question
Watch a rainy-day pitch — bad conditions show whether the structure is real

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain what improved question handling means, in your own words?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me how you handle a hard question — in the field or in roleplay.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you handle questions this way every day, not just on good days?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you do this on your own, without a coach reminding you?

2|Leading by Example.trainee_content:
You lead by example in how you act and what you produce. You are a walking example of what good looks like.

Before anyone gives you a team, you're already setting the standard: on time, prepared, positive, putting up numbers.

People copy what they see long before they follow what they're told.
what_good_looks_like: Leads by example in behaviour AND performance
Is a visible example of WGLL
Standard holds on bad days, not just good ones
how_measured: Coach watches them across a full week
Other BAs point to them as the example
Behaviour and numbers both at standard
leader_coaching_notes: Point out who's watching them — newer BAs copy everything
Praise the example with specifics, not 'good job'
One off-standard day is coaching; a pattern is a sit-down

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What does leading by example mean here? Explain it in your own words.
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me where you set the example today — in the field or in roleplay.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you set the example every day, including the bad ones?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you do it on your own, without a coach pushing you?

2|Personal Planning.trainee_content:
You have a clear weekly plan and you check it yourself — nobody has to remind you. And the plan comes from data, not feelings.

What you'll hit. Which days. What skill you're working on. What it pays. Written down before the week starts, checked while the week runs.
what_good_looks_like: Has a clear weekly plan and reviews it without being told
Builds the plan from data, not feelings
Plan has one education goal and one financial goal
how_measured: Weekly plan exists before Monday, on record
Mid-week self-check happens without a reminder
Plan gets more accurate week over week
leader_coaching_notes: Review their plan every Monday for a month, then spot-check
Ask what data sits behind each target — 'it felt right' isn't a source
Coach the review habit: a plan nobody rechecks is a wish

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Talk me through how you build your weekly plan.
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me this week's plan and how you're using it.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you plan and review like this every week?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you do it without a coach chasing you?

2|Problem-Solving Mindset.trainee_content:
When something goes wrong, you show up with a fix, not an excuse.

Break the problem down: what part can you control? Act on that part. Don't wait for someone else to fix what you can fix yourself.

The sector, the weather, the campaign — those are given. Your response is the one thing you own.
what_good_looks_like: Answers problems with fixes, not excuses
Breaks problems into what they can control and acts on it
Doesn't wait for someone else to fix what they can fix
how_measured: Problems come to you with a fix already attached
Watch how they handle a genuinely bad day
No excuse language in debriefs
leader_coaching_notes: When they bring a problem, ask for their fix before giving yours
Debrief a bad day: what could you control, and did you?
Model it — say your own controllables out loud

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What does a problem-solving mindset look like on the doors? Explain it.
assessment_prompts.skill: Tell me about a real problem this week and what you did about it.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you respond this way every day, even on rough ones?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you fix things yourself, without a coach stepping in first?

2|Profitability.trainee_content:
You know your personal breakeven and the industry averages you need to hit to represent the brand. And you use those numbers to decide what matters each day.

Breakeven is your needs divided by £55 — the BA fee for a standard £12 sign-up — turned into sign-ups a week. A professional knows exactly what a day has to produce — and plans backward from that number.
what_good_looks_like: Knows personal breakeven cold
Knows the industry averages needed to represent the brand
Uses these numbers to pick daily priorities and choices
how_measured: Can say their breakeven and averages without being asked
Daily choices clearly point back to the numbers
Weekly results tracked against breakeven
leader_coaching_notes: Quiz breakeven monthly — it changes and they should know it
Ask how today's plan covers the number
Tie every schedule choice back to profitability

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What's your breakeven, and what averages do you need to represent the brand?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me how today's plan covers your number.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you run your days off these numbers every day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you track them yourself, without a coach asking?

2|Rehash & Consolidation.trainee_content:
The sign-up isn't done when they say yes.

After the yes, remind them of the impact and the value. Make sure they fully understand what they agreed to — the Pop Quiz: monthly amount, how often, the start date (1st / 8th / 15th / 22nd) and why NDCS makes a Welcome Call. Then the 3 Thank You's. Leave them feeling good about the decision.

Consolidation is where quality is made. A confident supporter stays. A confused one cancels.
what_good_looks_like: Reminds the supporter of impact and value after the yes
Confirms they understand: what they agreed to, amounts, how often, dates
Leaves the supporter feeling good about their decision
how_measured: Quality KPIs: donations stick, cancellations low
Watched consolidations cover every confirmation point
Zero supporter callbacks or confusion complaints
leader_coaching_notes: Watch the 60 seconds AFTER the yes — that's the module
Tie their cancellation numbers to their consolidation habits
Roleplay the confirmation checklist until it's automatic

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What happens after the supporter says yes? Walk me through it.
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me a consolidation — in the field or in roleplay.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you consolidate every sign-up, every day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you do it without a coach reminding you?

2|Stage 2 \u2014 The Self Management Sta.trainee_content:
Stage 2 is where you stop needing a coach to walk you through every day. You run like a professional: your plan, your numbers, your standards — owned by you.

You move up on evidence, never on time served. And everything from Stage 1 still counts — Stage 2 sits on top of it.
what_good_looks_like: Evidence: a weekly plan for next week with one education goal and one financial goal
Evidence: can explain personal breakeven and acts in ways that back it up
Evidence: talks openly about their personal goals and vision
Evidence: at least one key KPI trending up over 1-2 weeks
how_measured: Keep hitting and building on every COD 1 standard
Miss a target for a full week and a written coaching plan follows within 24 hours
leader_coaching_notes: Go through the four evidence items in the weekly rhythm — agree the proof up front
Daily tools: Weekly Planning Template, Learning Library, Quality Checklist
If COD 1 standards slip, fix those before moving anything forward here

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What is the Self Management Standard, and what proof does it ask for?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me your evidence — plan, breakeven, goals, and KPI trend.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you holding this standard every day, week after week?
assessment_prompts.independence: Are you running it yourself, without a coach driving it?

2|Student Mentality.trainee_content:
Don't wait for feedback. Go get it. Ask your coach what to fix, listen, and change it the same day — without being told twice.

The people who advance fastest in this business are the best students. They ask, they listen, they change the habit that day, and they come back for more.
what_good_looks_like: Goes and asks for feedback and coaching instead of waiting for it
Fixes what was coached the same day, where people can see it
Never needs the same coaching twice
how_measured: Coaching lands first time — coach confirms it
The BA asks for feedback themselves, and it's on record
Skills getting better week after week
leader_coaching_notes: Test how fast it sticks: coach one thing, then watch the very next pitch
Praise them for asking, not just for applying
If they defend instead of listen, coach that first — it blocks everything else

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you tell me what student mentality means and why it matters?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me student mentality — take a piece of coaching and use it right now
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you act like a student every day, not just when I'm watching?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you go and ask for feedback yourself, without me pushing you?

2|Territory Awareness & Adaptability.trainee_content:
Every sector is different — how busy it is, who lives there, their background, how they connect, how old they are. You read that and change how you talk.

The same pitch does not work on every street. Stage 2 means you read the sector and adjust on your own, without being told.
what_good_looks_like: Knows how foot traffic, who lives there, and culture change from sector to sector
Changes their approach to fit the area without being told
Gets results in every kind of sector, not just the easy ones
how_measured: Results compared across very different sectors
Can say how today's sector changes how they pitch
Coach watches them adjust in the field
leader_coaching_notes: Before the first door, quiz them on the sector: who lives here, what works?
Compare their numbers across area types and coach the gap
Rotate them on purpose through very different sectors

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain how you read a sector and why you'd change your approach?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me — how would you pitch differently in two different sectors?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you adjust to the sector every day, whatever area you're in?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you read and adjust to the sector on your own, without me telling you?

2|The 8 Steps.trainee_content:
The 8 Steps are how a pro runs their day: attitude, time management, preparation, 100% effort, working territory, safeguarding your attitude, goals, taking control.

You can say what each one is for — and show them in the field. Stage 2 means they run on their own, no one watching over you.
what_good_looks_like: Can say what each of the 8 Steps is for
Shows them in the field without being told
Uses the steps to work out what went wrong on a rough day
how_measured: Talks through all 8 and what each is for — not just the names
Watched in the field against the steps
Their end-of-day reviews name specific steps
leader_coaching_notes: Quiz what each step is for, not the order — reciting isn't knowing
After a rough day, ask which step slipped
Coach one step per week until all eight are habits

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you walk me through the 8 Steps and what each one is for?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me the 8 Steps working in your day, in the field or in roleplay
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you run the 8 Steps every day, not just on good days?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do the 8 Steps run on their own, without me reminding you?

2|Using Numbers to Self-Coach.trainee_content:
Your numbers tell you where your day leaks — approaches, conversations, or closes. Read them, find the leak, and fix it yourself before anyone has to tell you.

That's what self-coaching means: the data shows the problem, and you act on it.
what_good_looks_like: Uses their own numbers to work out what's going wrong
Acts on what the numbers say without being told
Explains their performance in numbers, not feelings
how_measured: Their read of the problem matches what the data shows
They act on their own read, on their own steam
Their KPIs improve because of changes they made themselves
leader_coaching_notes: Hand them their own week and ask for the story in it
Check the action: spotting the problem without changing anything means nothing
Wean them off waiting for you to read their numbers for them

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain how you use your numbers to coach yourself?
assessment_prompts.skill: Take your own numbers right now — what's the leak and what do you do about it?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you check and act on your numbers every day?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you read your own numbers without waiting for me to do it?

3|Building Independence.trainee_content:
Your role is to build people who think and act on their own. As they get better, step back — pull the support away bit by bit as they grow.

Coach in a way that builds skill, not reliance on you. You're replacing yourself, not collecting people who can't move without you.
what_good_looks_like: Builds people who think and act on their own
Pulls support back step by step as people grow
Builds skill, not reliance — works to replace themselves
how_measured: The BAs they coach make the right call without checking first
The support they give visibly drops off over the weeks
The team runs a clean day with them not there
leader_coaching_notes: Count how often their people check in — dependency has a sound
Plan the support step-downs together, with dates
Coach the question-back habit: 'what would you do?'

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain how you build a BA's independence, step by step?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me — coach a teammate in a way that builds their own thinking
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you stepping back from your people week after week, not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you build independence in your team without anyone pushing you to?

3|Data-Driven New Starter Development.trainee_content:
Check your new starters' numbers every day and let them guide your coaching. Track the key numbers for each starter and act early when something is off.

Day-3 data predicts week-2 results — if you're reading it. Don't wait for the slump to show up in sign-ups.
what_good_looks_like: Uses numbers every day to guide new starter coaching
Tracks the key numbers for each starter
Acts early when a starter's numbers slip
how_measured: Coaching choices clearly point back to starter data
Steps in early — dated before the slump showed
Starters staying on and getting up to speed fast
leader_coaching_notes: Ask what the data says about each starter, every day in week one
Walk back through a lost starter: when did the data first warn you?
Coach the early warning numbers, not just sign-ups

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain how you use a starter's numbers to guide their coaching?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me — take a starter's numbers and tell me what you'd coach today
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you checking starter data every day, week after week?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you run this off the data yourself, without anyone chasing you?

3|Diagnosing Sign-Up Problems.trainee_content:
When a BA is struggling, find exactly where in the 5 Steps they leak. Then work out what kind of problem it is: activity, skill, or mindset. They're not the same thing.

The diagnosis decides the cure. More doors, a drilled skill, or a reset attitude are three different fixes — pick the right one, and coach changes you can track.
what_good_looks_like: Points at exactly which of the 5 Steps is leaking
Tells apart activity, skill, and mindset problems
Coaches fixes you can track against the diagnosis
how_measured: Their diagnosis matches what the data later confirms
The fixes can be tracked — and are tracked
The BAs they coach recover, and the numbers show it
leader_coaching_notes: Have them diagnose from watching, then check the numbers together
Quiz the three problem types on real cases
Watch for one-size-fits-all coaching — it means no diagnosis happened

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain how you find where a BA is leaking in the 5 Steps?
assessment_prompts.skill: Take a struggling BA — diagnose the problem and tell me the fix
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do your diagnoses hold up week after week, not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you spot and fix these problems yourself, without anyone flagging them?

3|Emotional Control Under Pressure.trainee_content:
When things get hard, you respond — you don't react. There's a gap between what happens and what you do next. Use it.

Don't dodge tough talks about underperformance. Have them.

Set a calm tone for the team on hard days. Pressure shows who the leader really is, and your team reads your face before they read the numbers.
what_good_looks_like: Responds instead of reacting under pressure
Doesn't dodge tough talks about underperformance
Stays calm and sets the tone on hard days
how_measured: Seen staying calm in genuinely hard moments
Tough talks happen on time, not put off
Team stays steady when results dip
leader_coaching_notes: Talk through their last pressure moment: what they felt vs. what they showed
Roleplay the conversation they're dreading
Watch the team's energy on a bad day — it copies the leader's

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain to me, in plain words, what emotional control under pressure means?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me — how would you stay in control while coaching a teammate through a rough moment?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you keep your cool every week, on bad days too — not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you hold yourself steady without a coach or teammate having to remind you?

3|Emotional Regulation.trainee_content:
Coach the behaviour, not the person. Don't let your feelings get pulled in.

When someone gets defensive or pushes back, stay calm. The moment coaching gets personal, it stops being coaching.
what_good_looks_like: Coaches the behaviour without getting emotionally pulled in
Stays calm when someone gets defensive or pushes back
Separates the person from the performance, every time
how_measured: Seen staying calm when coaching someone who pushes back
No relationships hurt by coaching talks
Team brings problems early — a sign coaching feels safe
leader_coaching_notes: Roleplay a defensive BA and watch how they hold up
Talk through any conversation that got heated: where did it turn?
When you see them stay calm in a hard moment, praise it by name

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain to me what emotional regulation means when you're coaching someone?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me — how do you stay calm when a teammate gets defensive with you?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you keep that calm every week, in every coaching talk — not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you manage your own reactions without anyone having to prompt you?

3|High-Clarity Team Meetings.trainee_content:
Plan your team meetings. Give them a structure and a clear point.

Everyone should walk out knowing three things: what we're doing, why, and what's expected of them next.

And the meetings run the same whether you're up or down. Your mood and this week's numbers don't get a vote.
what_good_looks_like: Meetings are planned and structured, with a clear point
Everyone leaves knowing what, why, and what to do next
Meetings run the same whatever the mood or the numbers
how_measured: Runs a team huddle that shows structure and clear direction
Quick check after: can people say what the actions are?
Meetings still happen on schedule in bad weeks
leader_coaching_notes: Sit in monthly; score structure, clarity, energy
Test what stuck: ask someone who attended for the three actions
Watch a bad-week meeting — that's where you see if it holds

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain to me what makes a team meeting high-clarity?
assessment_prompts.skill: Walk me through how you'd run a huddle so everyone leaves knowing their actions.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do your meetings run the same every week — good weeks and bad?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you plan and run these meetings yourself, without anyone chasing you?

3|Networking.trainee_content:
Build relationships past your own team. Don't wait for people to come to you.

Find the high performers and learn from them on purpose. It's the fastest way to grow.

The best leaders are built from a dozen borrowed strengths. Go collect them.
what_good_looks_like: Builds relationships past their own team without being asked
Learns from high performers on purpose
Puts what they borrow to work — you can see it
how_measured: Real relationships across teams and offices
Can name what they learned and who they learned it from
Borrowed techniques showing up in their own game
leader_coaching_notes: Ask who they learned from this month — there should be a name
Connect them on purpose with someone strong where they're weak
Talk through cross-office calls: what did you take from it?

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain to me why networking matters and how you do it?
assessment_prompts.skill: Tell me about something you learned from a high performer and how you used it.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you building these relationships every week, not just when it's easy?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you reach out and learn from others without anyone pushing you to?

3|Performance Conversations.trainee_content:
When someone's numbers slip, don't wait and don't dodge it. Talk to them early and say it straight.

Bring clarity, not frustration. They should leave knowing exactly what needs to change.

Then follow up. The talk means nothing if the change doesn't actually happen.
what_good_looks_like: Talks about performance gaps early, straight, and clearly
Clarity, not frustration — no sarcasm, no vague hints
Follows up so the change actually happens
how_measured: Performance issues handled on record, with dates
Numbers improve after the conversation
Team calls the feedback fair, even when it's hard to hear
leader_coaching_notes: Roleplay the conversation they're avoiding right now
Check the follow-up trail on their last three conversations
Coach clarity over comfort — being clear is the kind thing here

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain to me how to run a good performance conversation?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me — how would you tell a teammate their numbers have slipped?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you have these talks every week when they're needed — not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you start these conversations yourself, without being told to?

3|Personal Recruitment.trainee_content:
Own your own recruitment pipeline. Build it and keep it warm — don't wait for the office to hand you people.

Leaders who wait, plateau. Leaders who recruit their own team keep growing.

Know the cost of recruitment too. Every candidate who drops off has a price.
what_good_looks_like: Owns and builds their own recruitment pipeline
Keeps the pipeline warm — it's people, not a list
Knows the cost of recruitment
how_measured: Pipeline exists, stays current, and produces starters
Can walk through the cost of recruitment numbers
Referrals and self-sourced candidates coming in
leader_coaching_notes: Review their pipeline weekly like a sales number — it is one
Quiz them on cost per recruit and what a no-show really costs
Coach them to keep candidates warm, not just collect names

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain to me how your recruitment pipeline works and what a new recruit costs?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me your pipeline — who's in it and what's your next move with each?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you working that pipeline every week, not just when you're short on people?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you recruit on your own, or only when someone pushes you to?

3|Protecting Quality.trainee_content:
Protect quality every day, not just volume. And coach your people to put quality first at every stage of the sign-up.

A team that chases numbers without quality is borrowing from next month. Cancellations hand every shortcut back — with interest.
what_good_looks_like: Protects quality every day, not just volume
Coaches quality at every stage of the sign-up
Team quality KPIs hold even during big pushes
how_measured: Team 1st/3rd payment rates and cancellation numbers
Quality coaching moments seen in the field
No quality dips during high-volume weeks
leader_coaching_notes: Watch what they praise — praising volume alone teaches shortcuts
Go through their team's quality numbers together weekly
Roleplay the talk with a high-volume, low-quality BA

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain to me why quality matters as much as volume?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me — how would you coach a BA who's bringing in plenty of sign-ups but sloppy on quality?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do your team's quality numbers hold every week, even during a big push?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you guard quality on your own, without anyone having to flag it?

3|Sector Expertise.trainee_content:
Sector and site work has its own standard: territory allocation, sector meetings, end-of-day breakdowns, and data during the day.

As a Stage 3 leader, you lay the groundwork now. The full standard sits in the Sector/Site Leader (SL) stage of the COD. That stage opens up once you're actively running sectors.
what_good_looks_like: Knows what running a sector involves before doing it
Backs the sector leader's plan when working in their sector
Working towards the SL stage on purpose
how_measured: Check the Sector/Site Leader COD stage — that sheet is the standard
Watch how they pitch in when working inside someone else's sector
Readiness chat with their admin, written down
leader_coaching_notes: Show them the SL stage modules as a preview of what's coming
Hand them small pieces of sector responsibility before the full role
After a day in someone's sector, ask what they'd copy from how it was run

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you explain what sector work involves, in your own words?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me how you'd support a sector leader while working their sector.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you show sector know-how week after week, not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you push towards the SL stage without anyone reminding you?

3|Setting & Enforcing Standards.trainee_content:
You live the standard yourself first. Then you tell people clearly what good looks like — in quality, sign-ups, recruitment, and KPIs — and you hold them to it when it slips.

A standard you don't enforce is just a suggestion.
what_good_looks_like: Lives the standard themselves first
Tells the team clearly what good looks like (WGLL): quality, sign-ups, recruitment, KPIs
Holds people to the standard when it isn't met
how_measured: Can hold people to the office KPIs
The team knows the standards without having to ask
You see them enforce it — not just talk about it
leader_coaching_notes: Pick one standard: does the team know it, and what happened the last time it slipped?
Watch them enforce — firm tone, never personal
Their own behaviour is exhibit A. Check that first.

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What are our standards, and why do we hold them?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me how you'd call out a teammate who missed the standard.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you hold the standard every week, not just when it's easy?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you enforce standards without anyone telling you to?

3|Stage 3 \u2014 The Leader Standard.trainee_content:
Stage 3 means making other people successful. Your results now include everyone you coach — their skills, their quality, their independence.

The standard is protected at all times. The real test: does your team hold it when you're not there?

And your own numbers still have to hold while you coach. Leadership is added on top of your production, not instead of it.
what_good_looks_like: Evidence: can sign off a new starter on COD 1
Evidence: runs a team huddle with structure and clarity
Evidence: understands the cost of recruitment
Evidence: hits sector targets at least 3 days a week
Evidence: can hold people to the office KPIs
how_measured: Keeps every COD 2 standard going and builds on it
Protects quality at all times
Team holds the standards when their coach isn't there
Standard missed = act right away: retrain or take the responsibility back
Keeps their own numbers profitable while coaching
leader_coaching_notes: Check the evidence list every week — proof, not stories
Daily tools: Recruiting Pipeline Tracking, Onboarding Checklist
Watch the classic Stage 3 trap: coaching so much their own numbers die

assessment_prompts.knowledge: What does the Stage 3 standard ask of you, in your own words?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me how you coach a teammate to the Stage 3 standard.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you hit this standard week after week, not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you run at this standard without anyone pushing you?

3|Teaching the Sign-Up Process.trainee_content:
You can teach the sign-up process in clear steps anyone can repeat. You watch technique closely — in roleplay and in real time — and fix tone of voice, body language, and quality standards on the spot.

Teaching is a different skill from doing. Your task is to make the invisible parts of a good pitch visible, so someone else can copy them.
what_good_looks_like: Teaches the sign-up process in clear, repeatable steps
Watches technique closely in roleplay and in real time
Fixes tone of voice, body language, and quality on the spot
how_measured: Can sign off a new starter on COD 1
Before/after look at a new starter they coached
How fast their new starter gets a first sign-up, and early quality numbers
leader_coaching_notes: Watch them teach one step — clear instructions are the skill
Check it stuck: does the new starter still do it two days later?
Break the 'watch me' habit — the new starter has to do the reps

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Walk me through how you'd teach the sign-up process to a new starter.
assessment_prompts.skill: Coach me through one step right now, like I'm your new starter.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you coach the process well every week, not just once?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you coach new starters without being asked to?

3|Tracking Team Progression.trainee_content:
You track and review your team's progress every week, and you can see the trends and the weak spots.

You know who is moving up, who is stuck, and who is sliding back — and you turn that into clear coaching actions.
what_good_looks_like: Tracks and reviews team progress every week
Spots who is moving up, who is stuck, who is sliding back
Turns the data into clear coaching actions
how_measured: Weekly team review written down, with trends called out
Coaching actions trace back to the trends they spotted
Stuck BAs get caught and helped within two weeks
leader_coaching_notes: Check their read of the team monthly — do you see what they see?
Every stuck BA needs a named action; check for both
Compare their calls against the bells and quality data

assessment_prompts.knowledge: How do you track your team's progress, and why weekly?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me your team read: who's up, who's stuck, and what you'll do about it.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Does your weekly team review happen every week, not just some weeks?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you run the review without anyone chasing you?

3|Tracking the Recruitment Pipeline.trainee_content:
You keep an accurate, up-to-date picture of your recruitment pipeline.

You spot where people drop off and act on it to lift conversion and retention. Recruiting is a funnel — run it like one.
what_good_looks_like: Keeps an accurate, current picture of the pipeline
Spots where people drop out of the funnel
Acts to lift conversion and retention numbers
how_measured: Pipeline records match reality when spot-checked
Drop-off analysis exists with actions attached
Conversion rates going up, stage by stage
leader_coaching_notes: Walk the funnel together monthly: where do we lose people?
Check the records against what actually happened
One fix for one drop-off point at a time

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Explain your recruitment pipeline and where people drop off.
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me your pipeline right now — is it accurate and current?
assessment_prompts.consistency: Do you keep the pipeline updated every week, not in bursts?
assessment_prompts.independence: Do you manage the pipeline without anyone chasing you?

3|Weekly Planning Rhythm.trainee_content:
You plan the week ahead, every week, with clear priorities: what you'll do, how, and a review at the end. And you hand it in without anyone chasing you.

A leader's week is designed, not discovered.
what_good_looks_like: Plans the week ahead every week, with clear priorities
Does the work and the review without being chased
Picks the right priorities — impact over busywork
how_measured: Written weekly plan, handed in unprompted
The review happens and feeds next week's plan
Planned priorities match what the team actually needed
leader_coaching_notes: Read their plan on Monday and their review on Friday
Challenge the priorities, not just that a plan exists
If you had to chase the plan, that IS the coaching topic

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Why does a leader plan the week before it starts?
assessment_prompts.skill: Walk me through this week's plan and how you built it.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Has your plan landed every week, without gaps?
assessment_prompts.independence: Does the plan show up without anyone asking for it?

4|Advancing First-Generation Leaders.trainee_content:
Keep building first-generation leaders who can lead, coach, and make calls without leaning on you.

The real test at Stage 4 is not how good your leaders look standing next to you. It's how good they are when they're alone with a team and a decision to make.
what_good_looks_like: Their leaders run huddles, coaching, and standards without help
Decisions get made at the right level instead of coming up to them
The leadership bench gets deeper every month
how_measured: A first-generation leader signs off a new starter on Stage 1 with no help
Team performance holds when the Stage 4 steps away for a full day
Track record: people regularly advance out of their team
leader_coaching_notes: Track who they are building right now — there should always be a name
Push decisions back down: 'what would your coach do?'
Check each leader's independence monthly, not just their numbers

assessment_prompts.knowledge: Can you tell me what building first-generation leaders means and why it matters at this level?
assessment_prompts.skill: Show me how you build a first-generation leader, live, with your team watching.
assessment_prompts.consistency: Are you building your leaders to the standard week after week?
assessment_prompts.independence: Can you teach this to other leaders and build systems so it keeps happening?

4|Clear Expectations Meetings.trainee_content:
Set expectations with your leaders clearly and exactly. Say what the standard is and how it will be held — fast, and the same way every time.

Everyone should leave an expectations meeting knowing exactly what is required, by when, and what happens if it isn't met.
what_good_looks_like: Expectations are exact, measurable, and have a date
Every standard has a consequence — and it gets enforced
No one is ever surprised by an accountability conversation
how_measured: Leaders can repeat their expectations back correctly
There's a written record of expectations set and reviewed
When a standard is missed, enforcement actually happens

Check enforcement: find one missed standard and trace what happened next

4|Coach the Coach.trainee_content:
Watch another leader coach, then make their coaching better — and the proof shows up in the data.

Run the full loop: watch the coach, coach the coach, then check the change actually reached the BA on the doors.
what_good_looks_like: Watches coaching without taking over
Feedback to the coach is exact and about behaviour
The improvement shows up two levels down — in the BA's results
how_measured: A coached leader's BAs improve, and you can see it in the numbers
Before-and-after watches of the same leader coaching
The leader can say what they changed and why
leader_coaching_notes: Shadow a coaching session together, compare notes after
Have them coach one leader on one behaviour for two weeks — track it
Watch for hero-coaching: they improve the coach, not the BA directly
